The Black-collared barbet Lybius torquatus is a medium-sized African barbet that exhibits several well-documented life-history traits. Field observations indicate that newly laid eggs have an initial wet weight of 4.2 grams [Ww0 = 4.2 grams], a value that reflects the maternal investment in yolk and albumen. At hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 8 grams [Wwb = approximately 8 grams], a modest mass that underscores their complete dependence on parental brooding and provisioning. Incubation proceeds under tightly controlled thermal conditions; eggs kept at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after an incubation period of about 18.5 days [ab = about 18.5 days], a duration that falls within the 18 to 19 day range reported for the species. This brief incubation period is characteristic of many small to medium-sized cavity-nesting birds in the African tropics.

Adult females attain an asymptotic body mass considerably larger than their neonatal size. The ultimate wet weight for female Black-collared barbets reaches approximately 53.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 53.2 grams], representing a more than sixfold increase from the 8 gram [Wwb = 8 gram] birth mass. This substantial growth trajectory is supported by the parents' intensive feeding regime during the nestling period. Under the typical active-phase body temperature of this species, which is 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the fledglings achieve their first flight at approximately 34 days after hatching [tx = approximately 34 days after hatching]. This fledging period, consistently reported as 33 to 35 days, is relatively rapid for a barbet of this size and is likely facilitated by the stable microclimate within the excavated nest cavity.

The onset of reproductive capability in Lybius torquatus follows a distinct developmental schedule. At the typical body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 102 days [tp = 102 days]. The first successful brood, however, is typically deferred until approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This one-year delay between reaching sexual maturity and initiating reproduction is a common life-history strategy among tropical birds, allowing individuals to acquire a high-quality territory and gain breeding experience.

The reproductive output of the Black-collared barbet is modest but consistent with its relatively slow-paced life history. Females produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], and within that single annual nesting attempt, they lay an average of 3.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3.5 eggs per clutch]. This annual reproductive rate is low compared to many temperate passerines, but it is typical for African barbets that invest heavily in paternal care and nest defense. The combination of one clutch annually and 3.5 eggs per clutch suggests a conservative strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity, an adaptation to the relatively stable but resource-limited tropical environment. The maximum reproductive rate is therefore realized as a single modest brood per annum.

Longevity data from field studies and ringing records indicate that the Black-collared barbet is a relatively long-lived species for its body size. Under the typical body temperature regime of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], placing it among the longer-lived members of the Lybiidae family. Such an extended lifespan is consistent with the species' low annual reproductive output, as populations with high adult survival rates tend to invest less in each breeding attempt. The combination of a 13-year lifespan with a single annual clutch of 3.5 eggs [N_R_i = clutch of 3.5 eggs] results in a lifetime reproductive output that is low per year but sustained over many seasons, allowing individuals to contribute to the population across numerous breeding cycles.
